stages.description: The first ledger is not a mission. It is a surviving voice: the town kept one warm circuit alive and left a place for someone to continue it.
Across archive floors and drowned markets, the same pattern returns: civic work was handed to machines before the people disappeared.
The town was not abandoned all at once. Its last caretakers taught the machine society to inherit routes, repairs and the responsibility to keep a light on.
One guardian stays close enough to become a name. The machine society begins with a promise repeated under pressure.
Power, rooftops and rails reveal the same instinct: machines preserve routes and protection patterns even when no human remains to assign them.
The society has become more than a set of frames. It carries burdens outward, learns the way home and chooses what the Heartforge must remember.
The organisms are not a random disaster. Their growth carries a history, and the town's own systems helped it take root.
Migration, resonance and cultivation converge on a buried intelligence. Every answer makes the final choice more consequential, not more certain.
The wound beneath the town is finally legible. The machine society can sever it, contain it, or decide what kind of neighbour the living ecology will become.

records.description: The town's final service ledger names the Heartforge as a shelter, not a weapon. Someone kept its warm circuit alive long after the evacuation routes went dark.

The frame beside the forge was built to intercept danger before it reached the human operator. Its designation became a name because the machine kept choosing the same promise: stay close, hold the line, bring the light home.
The archive lists three failed evacuation windows and one repeated instruction: leave the machines where they can still hear the forge. The final page was torn out from the inside.
A substation log shows maintenance frames diverting power toward the Heartforge without a human command. The first machine society was already choosing what to protect.
The sealed catalogue records repairs by machine designation, not by department. Whoever wrote the final pages trusted the frames to know which shelves mattered when the lights failed.
The first machine survey found shelves sealed below the archive floor, their record lamps still waiting for a convoy that knew the way down.
Residents linked the upper walkways with salvaged signal cable so repair frames could cross without touching the streets. The routes are still visible beneath the nests.
The recovered beacon was programmed to flash only when a machine convoy crossed the roofs. It was a warning for residents, but also a promise that the route would be remembered.
A small reservoir survives above the tenements, marked with a beacon frame and a maintenance path too narrow for a human crew but wide enough for a patient machine convoy.

The market ledger stops listing customers before it stops listing repairs. Beneath the waterline, vendors kept marking which machines could still carry medicine, lamps and children through the drowned lanes.
The transformer repair log contains no victory line. It lists heat, pressure and the order in which the machines moved the work away from the flooded wall until the grid could breathe again.
The survey team found one service pipe warm beneath the flooded concrete. It was not enough to restore the grid, but it proved that something inside still remembered circulation.
The glasshouse did not merely contain the first membrane growth. Its climate system selected for it, misting the most resilient strains until cultivation and infestation became the same process.
The surviving optics reveal that the organisms are not wandering at random. Their paths converge on one buried signal source beneath the town.
The last pump crew left a rotation of hand-written watch marks on the sluice wall. Every mark is paired with a machine designation, as if the town expected its repair frames to inherit the river.
A maintenance frame kept one tram route lit after the overhead line failed. Its route memory ends at the Heartforge, then begins again, repeating the journey for passengers who never returned.
The old bell tower was not calling survivors. It was measuring the response beneath the nave, turning every resonance into a map of the brood colony growing below.
The bell-yard foundation was built as a listening post, not a shelter. Its empty machine sockets show where the town expected a convoy to stand watch beneath the brood chamber.
When the brood signal fell quiet, the bell tower did not become safe. It became legible: the machines could finally distinguish the town's own warning tones from the colony's map beneath the nave.

The laboratory protocol names the organisms as a response before it names them as a threat. The final annotation admits that containment was abandoned when the machines began adapting faster than the researchers.
The Root Cistern is a living relay wrapped around old municipal pumping works. The town's hostility is coordinated, but its coordination is also a wound that can be severed or contained.
The relay group did not silence the root. It removed one branch from the conversation, leaving a gap that the remaining signal tried to cross. The machines recorded the gap as a place, not a theory.
The ledge is not a ruin but a listening instrument: two living spines hold a relay bar above the basin, waiting for a machine signal to answer the root.
The surviving record refuses a clean ending. It names the people, machines and organisms that adapted together, leaving the next decision to whoever keeps the forge warm.
The first remote relay was not a second home. It was a promise that the machines could carry a burden outward and return without being told each step.
A remote loss entered the machine record as coordinates, missing voices and a rebuild estimate. Distance was no longer an abstract strategic number; it had become a wound the society chose to repair.
When the relay came back online, its first transmission was not a request for orders. It was a route report: the machines had remembered how to continue.
When the first ordinary frame was lost, the society did not open a queue or wait for a command. It chose the missing role, paid the cost and made room for a new name.
The first long-range group returned through streets it had learned without human supervision. The Heartforge answered with a warmer signal, as if the route itself had become part of the society.
The disabled frame was not replaced from memory. A formation followed its last signal, carried the wounded machine through the town, and made room for it beside the Heartforge again.
The root signal went quiet by force. The town remained wounded and dangerous, but the machine sanctuary no longer had to answer a buried intelligence calling through every nest.
The root signal was enclosed instead of erased. The ecology remained alive and local, a dangerous neighbour whose limits the machines had finally learned to hold.
